Integrating hyperfunctions over proper fibers

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

Integrating out a variable can remove a singularity or concentrate it at a critical value. For a hyperfunction, the construction must work even when no finite distributional order is available. We build integration using compact analytic representatives, then prove that only covectors with zero fiber component can survive. The proof keeps the original spherical measure when a higher-dimensional holomorphic representation is projected into fewer variables.

Let , be open, initially with , and put . A closed set is proper over when We assume this for . The integration convention is the scalar distribution convention with ordinary Lebesgue measure in the fiber coordinates.

The compact analytic-functional pushforward and its germ pairing are Analytic tests and real carriers, Proposition 7. Compact sections, arbitrary-cover gluing and extension are Hyperfunctions from local analytic sources, Proposition 4 and Theorems 3 and 8. The spherical field, carrier-seminorm limits and their boundary comparison are Holomorphic boundary values without growth bounds, Proposition 2 and Proposition 5(ii); its Theorem 6 gives the positive-dual wavefront bound. We use Continuing the spherical kernel, Theorem 6, with its complete exponential and derivative estimates. The finite-measure cone argument is Directional splitting and holomorphic compatibility, Lemma 1.

Compact representatives with controlled fiber support

Lemma 1 (a representative over an output patch). For every relatively compact open , the restriction of to has a compactly supported global hyperfunction representative on which is zero on . It is therefore represented by a compact real analytic functional .

Proof. Choose a bounded open with . Properness gives a compact set containing the fiber projection of . The section is zero on . Glue it with zero on ; these two open sets cover , since . Denote the resulting section by .

Now prescribe on and zero on the complement of the compact set . On their overlap both prescriptions are zero. They define a section on the open set The full extension theorem extends this section to , retaining all its prescribed values on . Its support is contained in , because its prescribed value on the complement is zero. Proposition 4 identifies this compact section with a unique analytic functional carried by that compact set. This is the required .

The specified zeros in (I2) are part of the construction. They ensure that an auxiliary fiber boundary cannot contribute to the integral.

Theorem 2 (proper integration). There is a well-defined linear operation for hyperfunctions with support proper over . On a patch as in Lemma 1 it is the restriction of the compact analytic functional It commutes with restriction of the output open set, satisfies and agrees with the existing proper integral of a distribution.

Proof. Formula (I3) is the previously proved pushforward under the analytic projection. Suppose are two representatives valid over . Their difference, as a global hyperfunction, is zero on . Its support is compact and lies outside this product. The compact-section theorem identifies the difference with an analytic functional carried by that actual support. Injectivity identifies this functional with . Its projection misses , so its pushforward restricts to zero on . Thus the definition is independent of the representative.

On overlaps the same argument applies after restriction to the common output patch. Arbitrary-cover gluing gives . The construction is linear: a finite union of proper supports is proper, and sums of representatives are representatives of sums. The same uniqueness proves restriction compatibility.

The set is closed in . Indeed, a convergent sequence in lies in a compact subset of ; its lifts in have a convergent subsequence by properness, whose limit is still in . If a neighborhood of an output point misses , the input is zero over that whole neighborhood, so its local representative may be zero. This proves (I4).

For a distributional input, choose smooth compact cutoffs in the output and fiber variables, equal to one on the smaller output patch and near all its relevant support fibers. Properness supplies one compact fiber neighborhood for this choice. The resulting compact distribution, extended by zero, is a representative allowed in Lemma 1. Its analytic-functional pushforward agrees with its ordinary compact distribution integral by Proposition 7 of the analytic-functional lesson. On the smaller output patch that integral is exactly the original proper integral. Independence of the representative proves the claimed agreement.

Proper fibers and the integration calculus

Theorem 6 (the full proper-support bound). Under (I1), The right side is closed off zero locally in the output cotangent bundle.

Proof. Fix an excluded pair . Choose the compact representative of Lemma 1 on an output neighborhood of . It agrees with on and is zero on . The zero extension actually vanishes off a compact subset of , so there is no artificial singularity at its boundary. Therefore every , for real , is absent from . Theorem 5 excludes from , whose restriction is .

For closedness, consider a sequence of pairs on the right converging to a nonzero output pair. Its base points lie in a compact output set. Every contributing input point belongs to , and properness bounds their fiber coordinates in a compact subset of . Take a convergent subsequence of those coordinates. The full input covectors converge to the nonzero pair , so closedness of supplies a lift of the limit.

Proposition 7 (derivatives, multipliers and repeated integration). For analytic on , If the support of on is proper over , integration over agrees with either iterated order.

Proof. Differentiation and analytic multiplication preserve support, so every input in (P2) is admissible. Choose a compact representative on an output patch, with its carrier inside the domain of the analytic germ of . The output derivative pairs with as , on both sides. The multiplier pairs as , on both sides. The fiber derivative pairs as . The compact-germ formulas and locality therefore prove (P2).

For repeated integration, properness over implies properness over and over : a compact set in either intermediate base has compact projection to , and the relevant support lies in the corresponding compact part of the original support. The projected support is proper over , by the compact-image property. Use Lemma 1 with the combined fiber to choose one compact representative agreeing with the input over a whole output patch and every fiber point. Its compact projection gives a representative for the intermediate integral, by the independence proved in Theorem 2. Each iterated order, and direct integration, gives exactly . Gluing proves the assertion.

Proof. The inverse diffeomorphism takes compact support pieces over a compact output set to compact sets, so the transformed support remains proper. Its block derivative has determinant ; its absolute value is analytic, since the determinant is nonzero with locally constant sign.

On compact representatives the existing coordinate pullback is . Choose . Since and , its value is . The local representatives may be chosen inside the coordinate domains; their proper fiber supports are compact there. This proves (P3) by independence and gluing.

For (P4), analytic multiplication gives and support in . This closed subset remains proper. Apply Theorem 6, retaining that support restriction on the possible fiber point.

If , properness means that the input support is compact. Its integral is the scalar , and there are no nonzero output covectors. If , integration is the identity. The derivative statements use empty sums or empty lists in these cases.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 (basic) — which point moments survive? Let be a point-carried analytic functional at , written in the proved convergent moment form Compute , and compute the integral of a fiber derivative.

Solution. Substitute . Every term with vanishes, so This series is legitimate by the original moment convergence on holomorphic germs; the subseries satisfies the same every-radius bounds. A derivative in a fiber coordinate pairs as minus the derivative of in that coordinate, hence integrates to zero. In particular is when , and zero otherwise, with the distributional derivative signs retained.

Exercise 2 (intermediate) — retaining a singular object exactly. Let be any compactly supported hyperfunction on , and let . Compute the integral of .

Solution. Its support is compact, and the existing iterated analytic-functional pairing gives since the second factor acts on the constant function with value one. This includes the nondistribution point functionals already constructed in the analytic-functional lesson. Thus proper integration is not limited to distributional inputs. The bound in (P1) allows the full wavefront of , with zero fiber component.

Exercise 3 (intermediate) — a vertical singularity integrates to zero. On , integrate , and check (P1).

Solution. Its support is proper over the first factor. Proposition 7 gives . Exact projection equality puts its wavefront at , : the nonzero derivative of a point delta has both one-dimensional singular directions, as seen from its polynomial Fourier transform. No such pair has zero fiber covector, so the right side of (P1) is empty. This is consistent with the computed zero.

Exercise 5 (advanced) — a fold creates an integrable singularity. Let , and integrate in . Compute the resulting distribution, determine its analytic wavefront, and compare with the horizontal conormals of the parabola.

Solution. The support is proper over . The analytic coordinate map has determinant one. Hence for a compact output test, The last equality follows by the substitutions and on the two open half-lines. First make the substitutions away from zero, then let that neighborhood shrink; the bound justifies the limit. There is no point mass added at zero. Thus the output is the locally integrable function with arbitrary value at its single undefined point.

It is analytic on each half-line and is not smooth at zero. Its ordinary wavefront there is nonempty by the proved wavefront projection theorem. Exercise 6 (basic) — a sufficient support hypothesis. Compare the ordinary fiber integrals of and on . What do they say about the role of properness?

Solution. Both supports are the whole plane and are not proper over . The integral of diverges, while the Gaussian integral proved in the supplied foundations gives . Properness supplies a construction for every hyperfunction meeting it. Its failure does not exclude additional input-specific integrals, as the Gaussian shows; the theorem does not assign a value to the divergent example.

Programme proofs and mathematical source

  • Hyperfunctions from local analytic sources, Proposition 4 and Theorems 3 and 8, gives compact representatives, gluing and extension with prescribed zeros. Analytic tests and real carriers, Theorem 2 and Proposition 7, gives moment expansions and the actual compact pushforward.
  • Holomorphic boundary values without growth bounds, Proposition 2, Proposition 5(ii) and Theorems 3 and 6, supplies the exact carrier and wavefront interfaces. Continuing the spherical kernel, Theorems 4–6, supplies continuation and exponential tails. Directional splitting and holomorphic compatibility, Lemma 1, supplies the finite-measure inward-cone argument.
  • Analytic substitution for hyperfunctions, Theorems 7 and 10 and Corollary 11, and Tensor directions and admissible hyperfunction products, Lemma 5 and Theorem 6, supply the coordinate, submersion and tensor comparisons. Keeping zero covectors in kernel operations, Theorem 2, is the existing distributional integral.
  • The supplied metric foundation, Sections 12–13, integration foundation, Sections 15–16, and complex contour foundation, CX7–CX11 and CMI6–CMI8, give the compactness, cutoffs, absolute integrals, substitutions and complex differentiation used above. The ordinary wavefront and Gaussian comparison proofs are in the complete Fourier and pullback reading, Sections 18.1–18.5.
  • Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I: Distribution Theory and Fourier Analysis, reprint of the second edition, Springer, 2003, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2, Theorems 8.5.4 and 8.5.4′ and the hyperfunction extension required in Section 9.3. The compact extension, closed-ball measure argument, exposition, examples, exercises and figure here are independently expressed.

General singular kernel action, kernel composition, convolution and the further support-normal assertions require their additional arguments. The proper integral and bound proved here supply their integration step.
